Title: LA Tournament Results (a.k.a. The Corrupter was sorta right)

Messages.Author: Robert Goudie
Messages.Body:
We played four V:TES tournaments at a Con in LA over Labor Day weekend.
Here's a few highlights.

1. If anyone still doubts the brain of our Steve "don't call me Tom"
Bucy (tb...@lainet.com) who has recently made bold statements regarding
the necessity of intercept (and other views that go against the flow),
you should know that he played in 3 tournaments (each with 25 players)
and finished in 1st place 2 times and got a 2nd place finish the other
time. He did this with three different decks. I played in two finals:
One I got 2nd place behind Steve, and the other, well, see below... I'm
sure that you'll doubt the quality of the other players but you
shouldn't.

2. Gangrel Infinite Loop decks. There were two. The first one was
OK. The guy took out his prey every time. And fast too. But never
went farther. Why play a deck that doesn't win? Now the other one
added a Toreador or two to play Distractions. His loop never broke. He
cycled through at least thirty cards for about 20 points in bleeds
before having to stop. I was ousted on the fourth turn of this final.
Once stopped it seemed to take 3 or 4 turns to get what he needed to
start again. After he ousted me, his new prey back bled him for seven
pool and then his grand prey Bum's Rushed and burned the famous vamp.
So, I agree that it did require a gang up situation and that is a
problem, but on the other hand, who cares? If you play these decks
you'll get one victory point and then die. However, I would still love
to see No Repeat Actions implemented.

3. Our newsgroups very own Chris Schorb has been following the Weenie
Vote Push talks and decided to try out his at the tournament. It was a
night tournament so there was only one round and then a final. After
the first round Chris was in agreement with The Corrupter (and other)
becuase he swept the table in 20 minutes (nobody from my playgroup or
other good players were at his table). In the final, Chris didn't even
have one Praxis Siezure go. He had a good player near him who
intercepted the votes. Anyway, I agree that these decks are a problem
if the table environment is a particular way. It seems to me that you
are taking a big chance playing this deck. I'd call a WVP a
one-trick-pony. (Note: I think Chris won 1st place anyway because time
ran out and he had one mroe blood than the other players!)

Robert

Hi Doug,

My admonishment to not doubt the quality of other players was in
reference to Steve Bucy's success at the tournaments. The finals were
packed with particularly high quality players and Steve was still
dominant. I freely admit that in the prelimary rounds there were many
poor players mixed in. Steve no doubt got several easy victory points
along the way.

There is an identifiable group that has dominated the tournaments at the
last 3 conventions. That group consists of 3 players from my playgroup
and 3 players from another playgroup. There are also 2 individuals from
neither group who make it to the finals often. The table that had the
WVP present in a preliminary round did not have any of the 8 players
that have consistanly been winners. At least 6 of these eight players
subscribe to the view that intercept is a necessary component in almost
any winning deck. So my comment was not a generalization but rather a
specific attempt to show that the players who have proven their quality
with repeated trips to the finals are the same ones who typically make
use of intercept. The 1st round table with the WVP present can
objectively be shown to have inferior players due to none of those
players having made consistant trips to the finals.

Messages.Body:
In article <50l2sv$b...@gozer.inri.com>, Johnny Tullner <j...@inri.com> wrote:

[Gangrel Infinite Loop described, snipped]

>I don't understand the decks you are describing. My Gangrel infinite

>At the very least I will oust 2 players on my 3rd or 4th turn. Once

>berserk w/fame/legendary there is no stopping it anyway.

>As far as I can tell it is immune to everything, the only thing that

>might stop it is a deck with *nothing* but wake ups and intercept.
>It's too fast for vote or bleed, and SCE stops combat and blocking.

Does nobody try to block the Rapid Healings? Note that when a Rapid
Healing is blocked, there is no combat, but rather the opportunity for
diablerie (& I'm sure the table would be more than happy to vote
it down). Can't Form of Mist or Earth Meld in that case, and you have
a max of +4 stealth (+1 inherent/+2 Earth Control/+1 Backways).

A decent Ravnos Ani/Chi intercept Apparition/Trap/Drawing out the Beast
combat deck should hose you just fine -- can't even Kiss the Fortitudinous
Ravnos.

Rapid Healing has always been the hole in Gangrel Infinite Loop -- mind
you, since it's only really addressable by a deck with Intercept and
Fortitude (namely Ravnos or Intercept Gangrel, or some really twisted
Ventrue variant), it's still degenerate as all get-out (and fully addressed
by SPTR).

Block the Rapid Healings when the vamp doesn't have enough blood to pull off
a Kiss, and you don't even need Fortitude. +5 intercept -- challenging, but
feasible.

Hi Ray,

The Gangrel Infinite Loop is done with a Gangrel (usually) who does an
action (probably bleed) and then after it is tapped it does a Force of
Will. The force of will sends the vampire to torpor after it bleeds.
If Fame is on the Vampire, the prey loses three pool. Next the vampire
does a Movement of the Slow Body which allows them to untap while in
torpor and at superior they also gain a blood. Finally the Gangrel does
a Rapid Healing which allows them to leave torpor at +1 Stealth and at
superior they gain a blood. At this point the circle is complete. The
Gangrel again does a bleed action and is tapped, etc. etc.

Robert Goudie

I find the underlined statement above quitefunny. In the tournaments I have
been in, one of the consistent players _never_ had any intercept in his
decks, yet got 1st in one, and 2nd or 3rd in the rest.

I have come to the conclusion, along with Curt Adams, I believe, that
intercept or its lack in a deck will be more valuable depending on the
regional uses of stealth. In area where NL or NL/GT have propogated,
tight stealthless rush would make intercept less valuable, while in other
areas with a CL background, the opposite is true (less 0 Stealth
attacks). Since the area will continue to build decks with these
principles in mind, you will see the above examples (my friend and Bucy)
being wildly disparate.

> 2. Gangrel Infinite Loop decks. There were two. The first one was

I guess I care. One of my goals is for an environment where any
particular deck can be made, and it will not require a gang-up
situation. Very few decks can win against a gang-bang attack. The
problem I have with this situation is that while gang-bangs should happen
to any particular deck that looks like it might run away with the game,
if an environment propogates a deck type where this situation is constant
or near-constant, that environment is broken. In DCI, repeat actions are
still a problem, and even if one occasionally falters (see Gangrel deck
above), the fact is that in DCI their faltering is the exception and not
the rule.

> 3. Our newsgroups very own Chris Schorb has been following the Weenie

> have one Praxis Siezure go. He had a good player near him who

Particular situations do not prove a rule. Try the deck again and again
in different seating arrangements, against different players, etc.. In
my own testing, (roughly 20 games against multiple different opponents)
except against decks where intercept was the focus of its first prey, it
won ~93% of the games (14 out of 15). In the games with an interceptor
prey, it won 40% of the games (2 out of 5), still higher than the average
of 20%.

> Anyway, I agree that these decks are a problem
> if the table environment is a particular way. It seems to me that you
> are taking a big chance playing this deck. I'd call a WVP a
> one-trick-pony. (Note: I think Chris won 1st place anyway because time
> ran out and he had one mroe blood than the other players!)

I'd call a WVP deck a OTP as well, but in an environment without good vote
pushing restrictions of some kind, the risk is minimal. You get hurt by
an intercepter prey, but still win more often than a typical deck.

I've been thinking about this since the original post. IME, the counter
to intercept decks is 0 stealth action decks, especially 0 stealth combat
decks (rush or B&B). (Although 0 stealth bleed-and-run-away works too)
With the original set, any high-intercept deck jams outrageously facing
such a thing and will get beaten to a pulp.

However, there is one new card which could trash this dynamic, our old
friend Thought Betrayed. If that first combat happens under TB from the
interceptor, the traditional result (interceptor goes to torpor) is
inverted (interceptee goes to torpor). While there are certainly
Dominateless intercept combat decks, Tremere intercept combat is the most
common one I see, and if you can't handle one of the most common
archetypical decks, you're not going to do well.

Anyway, I'm wondering if this is the reason some groups don't see rush/B&B
combat cutting intercept combat down to size.

Curt Adams (curt...@aol.com)

Messages.Author: The Corrupter
Messages.Body:
On Wed, 4 Sep 1996, Ray Babbitt wrote:

> Robert Goudie wrote:
> > 2. Gangrel Infinite Loop decks.

> OK, I'm new at this game. Can you please explain the idea behind this

> deck? What do you mean by "infinite loop?" I'm assuming that you are
> not referring to recycling your library, as I haven't seen many cards
> that let you retrieve cards from your ash heap. Is this "infinite loop"
> duplicatable in other decks, or is it specific to Gangrels?

This deck does not exactly "recycle" cards from the ashheap. The
Infinite Loop is actually more finite than infinite, but goes as follows:

Gangrel:
Act (somehow) + Force of Will + Movement of the Slow Body +
Rapid Healing (end result, a tapped vampire, able to start the loop again
with Force of Will)
Act (somehow) + Freak Drive + act + Freak Drive + ... + Refill
blood (via Hospitality, Restoration, Aaron's Feeding Razor) + Freak
Drive (end result, an untapped vampire able to start the loop again)
Ventrue: As the 2nd Gangrel example
Slight Variations: Use Majesty to untap from blocked actions.
Use Voter Captivation to refill.
Toreador often do the same as a combination Ventrue/Gangrel S:CE effect.

In any case, in more plain English, an Infinite Loop deck is one that
sets up a situation that can be repeated again and again in the same
turn, resulting in near infinite actions (only limited by the size of the
deck). Most people (though not all) consider this degenerate. The DCI
uses a restricted list to stop this problem (putting a 6 card cap on
cards capable of causing untaps offensively, and on massive blood refill
(Hospitality)). This "solution", however, doesn't address several
problems and creates some new ones (another thread). Another solution
(part of what is called the Golden Tenets, the most widely used house
rules along with Card Limits) puts a limit on actions: No action may be
repeated more than once per minion per turn. It has been argued that
this solution also hamstrings some deck creation (notably tap-out decks
using S:CE) but this has been shown to be unfounded.

Messages.Author: Thetmes
Messages.Body:
The reason the results of the L.A. tournament where so disparate was not
because I had intercept in all my decks. In fact one of the winning decks
(a political deck) had virtually no intercept in it. The reason I excelled
was the growing lack of intercept in others decks since the DCI rules have
been used. All of my decks had two common elements: lots of stealth, and
lots of combat defense (S:CE, elysium, obedience). Almost everyone was
relying on deflection (or nothing at all) for protection from S/B. With me
bleeding 3 or 4 times a turn at 2 or 3, plus my deflections, they seemed
to run out of deflections quickly. Once out of deflections I would bleed
them out of the game by playing just +1 stealth on every bleed (including
return to innocence). Most of the time it was shockingly easy.

On the other hand, one of my decks held off one of the nastiest S/B decks
I have ever seen for many turns with a combination of 2nd traditions, cats
guidance, and deflections. He had swept his way to the final, and was
quite surprised to see me block his first bleed for 6 at +3 stealth.
Without the 12 intercept cards in that deck I would have been out of
defections and dead very soon.

There where quite a few rush decks around but they couldn't do enough
damage to win consistently with all the end combat (even TB) stuff around.
An excellent Assimite deck had a major effect on one of the final round
games but he failed to get a victory point. Lots of people where using
Tremere (or Malks) with Talbot's chainsaw, Rutor's hand, and sometimes
Hiedleberg castle. Nothing like Talbot's chainsaw coming at you three
times a turn! But even these guys couldn't take out enough vamps to win
(though one finished third). All the Brujah, Gangrel, and Ravnos rush
decks never even made it to the finals.

In short, the presence of intercept (at least in two of my decks) set me
apart from most of the other players, but it was really the overall lack
of intercept in L. A. that enabled me to do so well.
